title: Roles and Responsibilities - FedRAMP Legacy Documentation
content:
- **Page status / scope**
  - “This page contains legacy content for reference only!”
  - “June 24, 2026: All materials in the FedRAMP Legacy Documentation site are intended only for reference during the transition to FedRAMP's Consolidated Rules for 2026.”
  - “Humans and AI services must be careful referencing any content in https://fedramp.gov/legacy because FedRAMP is actively transitioning away from these processes and materials.”

- **Role-assignment / responsibility matrix**
  - **CSP**
    - **SSP**: “Develop SSP documentation using FedRAMP templates*. Validate work prepared by advisors (if applicable).”
    - **SAP**: “Review and approve the SAP. Sign the SAP.”
    - **SAR**: “Provide required artifacts and evidence to the 3PAO during assessment. Work with the 3PAO to identify risks that must be remediated or mitigated prior to authorization.”
    - **POA&M**: “Create and maintain a POA&M that aligns with _FedRAMP's POA&M Template. Implement monthly ConMon. Use the POA&M to track and manage risks.”
  - **3PAO**
    - **SSP**: “As an advisor, develop the SSP documentation**. As an assessor, validate the SSP documentation is complete and accurate**.”
    - **SAP**: “Coordinate with CSP to define assessment scope and methodology. Deliver SAP and security test case procedures using FedRAMP templates***. Sign the SAP. Deliver penetration test plan that aligns with FedRAMP's guidance.”
    - **SAR**: “Perform assessment of the CSO according to FedRAMP guidelines. Draft a SAR that aligns with the SSP/SAP detail and describes the findings of the assessment***. Deliver the SAR to the CSP.”
    - **POA&M**: “Validate the POA&M detail for a CSO as part of the annual assessment. If performing POA&M activities on behalf of a CSP, assume all CSP responsibilities for POA&M management.”

- **Security operations roles / task ownership / approvals**
  - CSPs and 3PAOs should “understand and agree on the division of roles and responsibilities with respect to the development of an authorization package.”
  - “Although CSPs do not develop the SAP and SAR, they are responsible for reviewing and approving these documents.”
  - “For this reason, this Playbook includes several tips on how to review the SAP and SAR for completeness, correctness, and consistency.”

- **Template / required document field names and exact required items**
  - **CSPs are required to use FedRAMP templates for:**
    - “the SSP”
    - “security controls rules of behavior (RoB)”
    - “information system contingency plan (ISCP)”
    - “control implementation summary (CIS)”
    - “customer responsibility matrix (CRM) workbook”
    - “integrated inventory workbook”
    - “POA&M”
    - “cryptographic modules table”
  - **CSPs develop their own:**
    - “policies and procedures”
    - “user guides”
    - “incident response plans”
    - “configuration management plans”
  - “Additional guidance on each of these required documents is provided in Section 12 of the SSP template.”
  - **3PAOs are required to use FedRAMP templates for:**
    - “the SAP”
    - “security test case procedures”
    - “SAR”
    - “risk exposure table (RET)”

- **Reviewer / authorization responsibilities**
  - “CSPs are responsible for reviewing and approving” the “SAP and SAR.”
  - “CSPs do not develop the SAP and SAR.”
  - “For this reason, this Playbook includes several tips on how to review the SAP and SAR for completeness, correctness, and consistency.”
  - “CSPs and 3PAOs should understand and agree on the division of roles and responsibilities with respect to the development of an authorization package.”

- **Exact notes / conditions / conventions**
  - “Validate work prepared by advisors (if applicable).”
  - “As an advisor, develop the SSP documentation**.”
  - “As an assessor, validate the SSP documentation is complete and accurate**.”
  - “Coordinate with CSP to define assessment scope and methodology.”
  - “Deliver SAP and security test case procedures using FedRAMP templates***.”
  - “Deliver penetration test plan that aligns with FedRAMP's guidance.”
  - “Perform assessment of the CSO according to FedRAMP guidelines.”
  - “Draft a SAR that aligns with the SSP/SAP detail and describes the findings of the assessment***.”
  - “Deliver the SAR to the CSP.”
  - “Validate the POA&M detail for a CSO as part of the annual assessment.”
  - “If performing POA&M activities on behalf of a CSP, assume all CSP responsibilities for POA&M management.”
  - “Implement monthly ConMon.”
  - “Use the POA&M to track and manage risks.”

- **Footnote / approval / escalation-related conventions**
  - “*** Per the A2LA R311: Specific Requirements - FedRAMP, 3PAOs contracted to provide advisory services cannot provide assessment services for the same CSO for a period of two years.*”
  - The page contains “**” and “***” markers in the matrix, but no separate inline explanation is provided on the page beyond the A2LA R311 note above.

title: REV_4_FedRAMP-SSP-Moderate-Baseline-Template.docx
content:
- **Role-assignment / responsibility matrix / RACI / responsibility-specific facts**
  - No explicit “RACI” or “RACI matrix” term appears in the page.
  - **Table 13‑2. Control Origination and Definitions** defines responsibility/origination categories:
    - **Service Provider Corporate** — “A control that originates from the CSP Name corporate network.”
    - **Service Provider System Specific** — “A control specific to a particular system at the CSP Name and the control is not part of the standard corporate controls.”
    - **Service Provider Hybrid** — “A control that makes use of both corporate controls and additional controls specific to a particular system at the CSP Name.”
    - **Configured by Customer** — “A control where the customer needs to apply a configuration in order to meet the control requirement.”
    - **Provided by Customer** — “A control where the customer needs to provide additional hardware or software in order to meet the control requirement.”
    - **Shared** — “A control that is managed and implemented partially by the CSP Name and partially by the customer.”
    - **Inherited from pre-existing FedRAMP Authorization** — “A control that is inherited from another CSP Name system that has already received a FedRAMP Authorization.”
  - Repeated control tables include fields:
    - **Responsible Role**
    - **Implementation Status (check all that apply)**
    - **Control Origination (check all that apply)**
    - **Part a / Part b / Part c / Part d / Part e / Part f / Part g**
    - **Parameter ...** fields where applicable
  - **Table 9‑1. Personnel Roles and Privileges** includes role-based ownership/privilege data:
    - Columns: **Role**, **Internal or External**, **Privileged (P), Non-Privileged (NP), or No Logical Access (NLA)**, **Sensitivity Level**, **Authorized Privileges**, **Functions Performed**
    - Example roles explicitly listed:
      - **UNIX System Administrator** — Internal — P — Moderate — Full administrative access (root) — Add/remove users and hardware, install and configure software, OS updates, patches and hotfixes, perform backups
      - **Client Administrator** — External — NP — N/A — Portal administration — Add/remote client users. Create, modify and delete client applications
      - **Program Director** — Internal — NLA — Limited — N/A — Reviews, approves and enforces policy
    - It explicitly states the table must include **all roles including systems administrators and database administrators** and also **web server administrators, network administrators and firewall administrators** if they can configure a device or host impacting the CSP service offering.
    - It also states the table must include whether roles are fulfilled by **foreign nationals** or **systems outside the United States**.
  - **Information System Owner** section:
    - “The following individual is identified as the system owner or functional proponent/advocate for this system.”
    - Table fields: **Name**, **Title**, **Company / Organization**, **Address**, **Phone Number**, **Email Address**
  - **Authorizing Official** section:
    - “The Authorizing Official is determined by the path that the CSP is using to obtain an authorization.”
    - **JAB P-ATO:** “FedRAMP, JAB, as comprised of member representatives from the General Services Administration (GSA), Department of Defense (DoD) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS)”
    - **Agency ATO:** “Agency Authorizing Official name, title and contact information”
    - “The Authorizing Official (AO) or Designated Approving Authority (DAA) for this information system is the *Insert AO information as instructed above*.”
  - **Other Designated Contacts** section:
    - “AOs should use the following section to identify points of contact that understand the technical implementations of the identified cloud system.”
    - “AOs should edit, add, or modify the contacts in this section as they see fit.”
    - Table fields: **Name**, **Title**, **Company / Organization**, **Address**, **Phone Number**, **Email Address**
    - “The following individual(s) identified below possess in-depth knowledge of this system and/or its functions and operation.”
    - Separate named table types:
      - **Information System Management Point of Contact**
      - **Information System Technical Point of Contact**
      - **Point of Contact**
  - **Assignment of Security Responsibility** section:
    - “The Information System Security Officers (ISSO), or their equivalent, identified below, have been appointed in writing and are deemed to have significant cyber and operational role responsibilities.”
    - Table type: **CSP Name Internal ISSO (or Equivalent) Point of Contact**
    - Table type: **AO Point of Contact**
  - **System Security Plan Approvals** section:
    - **Cloud Service Provider Signatures**
    - Repeated approval blocks with fields:
      - **Name**
      - **Date**
      - **Title**
      - **Cloud Service Provider**
      - **CSP Name**
  - **System Status** choices:
    - **Operational**
    - **Under Development**
    - **Major Modification**
    - **Other**
  - **Cloud service / deployment / leverage fields**
    - **Service Provider Architecture Layers**:
      - **Software as a Service (SaaS)** — Major Application
      - **Platform as a Service (PaaS)** — Major Application
      - **Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)** — General Support System
      - **Other** — Explain: Click here to enter text.
    - **Service Provider Cloud Deployment Model**:
      - **Public**
      - **Private**
      - **Government Only Community**
      - **Hybrid**
    - **Leveraged Authorizations** table fields:
      - **Leveraged Information System Name**
      - **Leveraged Service Provider Owner**
      - **Date Granted**
      - Instruction says if none, write **“None”** in the first column.
  - **Personnel role examples and explicit responsibility language in controls**
    - **AC-1** and many other controls use “organization-defined personnel or roles” as a placeholder.
    - **AC-2** explicitly requires:
      - approvals by organization-defined personnel or roles for account creation requests
      - account managers
      - monitoring use of accounts
      - notifications to account managers when accounts no longer required, users terminated/transferred, or usage/need-to-know changes
      - reviews of accounts at least annually
      - process for reissuing shared/group account credentials
    - **AC-2 (7)**: privileged user accounts administered via role-based access scheme; monitors privileged role assignments; takes organization-defined actions when no longer appropriate.
    - **AC-2 (12)**: monitors account atypical use and reports atypical usage to organization-defined personnel or roles; required for privileged accounts.
    - **AC-5**: separates organization-defined duties; documents separation of duties; defines access authorizations to support separation of duties.
    - **AC-6 (2)**: users with access to all security functions use non-privileged accounts/roles when accessing non-security functions; examples of security functions listed include establishing system accounts, configuring access authorizations, setting events to be audited, setting intrusion detection parameters, system programming, system and security administration, other privileged functions.
    - **AC-6 (5)**: restricts privileged accounts to organization-defined personnel or roles.
    - **AC-6 (9)**: audits execution of privileged functions.
    - **AC-6 (10)**: prevents non-privileged users from executing privileged functions, including disabling/circumventing/altering security safeguards.
    - **AU-5(a)** alerts organization-defined personnel or roles on audit processing failure.
    - **AU-6(b)** reports findings to organization-defined personnel or roles.
    - **AU-9 (4)** authorizes access to management of audit functionality to only organization-defined subset of privileged users.
    - **PE-13 (2)** fire suppression device activation notifications to organization-defined personnel or roles and organization-defined emergency responders.
    - **IR-9(b)** alerts organization-defined personnel or roles of the information spill using a method of communication not associated with the spill.
    - **IR-9(1)** assigns organization-defined personnel or roles with responsibility for responding to information spills.
    - **SI-4(v)** provides organization-defined information system monitoring information to organization-defined personnel or roles.
    - **SI-5(j)** disseminates alerts/advisories/directives to system security personnel and administrators with configuration/patch-management responsibilities.
    - **SI-6(c)** notifies system administrators and security personnel of failed security verification tests.
    - **SI-11(b)** reveals error messages only to organization-defined personnel or roles.

- **Approvals / authorization / reviewer responsibilities**
  - **System Security Plan Approvals** requires signature blocks; no actual signer names are filled in.
  - **Authorizing Official**:
    - JAB P-ATO path uses FedRAMP/JAB comprised of GSA, DoD, DHS member representatives.
    - Agency ATO path uses agency Authorizing Official name/title/contact information.
    - AO or DAA is the authorizing official title used.
  - **CA-2**:
    - Results of security control assessment provided to organization-defined individuals or roles **to include the FedRAMP Program Management Office (PMO)**.
    - For JAB Authorization, assessment must use an **accredited Third Party Assessment Organization (3PAO)**.
    - The control allows assessment results acceptance by **any FedRAMP Accredited 3PAO** when conditions of the **JAB/AO in the FedRAMP Repository** are met.
    - Assessment products and test plans are approved/accepted by **JAB/AO** before initiating testing.
  - **CA-3**:
    - Interconnections authorized through **Interconnection Security Agreements**.
    - Reviews and updates Interconnection Security Agreements **at least annually and on input from FedRAMP**.
    - Table 13‑3 is **CA-3 Authorized Connections**.
  - **CA-5**:
    - Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) must be provided **at least monthly**.
  - **CA-6**:
    - Security authorization updated in accordance with **OMB A‑130 requirements** or when a significant change occurs.
    - Significant change definition referenced to **NIST SP 800‑37 Revision 1, Appendix F**.
    - Types of changes impacting risk posture are approved and accepted by **JAB/AO**.
  - **CA-7**:
    - operating system scans: **at least monthly**
    - database and web application scans: **at least monthly**
    - all scans performed by Independent Assessor: **at least annually**
  - **CA-8**:
    - penetration testing: **at least annually**
  - **CP-2**:
    - contingency plan reviewed and approved by organization-defined personnel or roles
    - copies distributed to organization-defined key contingency personnel and organizational elements
    - JAB authorizations: contingency lists include designated FedRAMP personnel
  - **CP-4**:
    - contingency plan tested **at least annually** using **functional exercises**
    - test plans provided to FedRAMP prior to initiating testing
    - test plans approved and accepted by **JAB/AO** before testing
  - **IR-3**:
    - tests incident response capability **at least annually**
    - for JAB authorization, test plans provided to **JAB/AO annually**
    - test plans approved and accepted by **JAB/AO** prior to test commencing
  - **IR-8**:
    - incident response plan reviewed **at least annually**
    - distributed to FedRAMP-defined incident response personnel and organizational elements; list includes designated FedRAMP personnel
  - **RA-2**:
    - security categorization decision reviewed and approved by **AO or authorizing official designated representative**
  - **RA-3**:
    - risk assessment results disseminated to organization-defined personnel or roles
    - review/update risk assessment **in accordance with OMB A‑130 requirements or when a significant change occurs**
    - for JAB authorizations, includes **all Authorizing Officials; for JAB authorizations to include FedRAMP**
  - **RA-5**:
    - scans operating systems/infrastructure, web applications, and databases **once annually** by an accredited independent assessor
    - high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within **30 days**
    - moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within **90 days**
    - low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within **180 days**
    - high vulnerability scan findings require RA-5(8)
    - results shared with organization-defined personnel or roles
    - for JAB authorizations, include all Authorizing Officials; for JAB authorizations to include FedRAMP
  - **SA-4**:
    - must comply with **FAR Subpart 7.103**, **Section 889 of the John S. McCain NDAA for FY 2019 (Pub. L. 115-232)**, and **FAR Subpart 4.21**
    - Common Criteria (**ISO/IEC 15408**) evaluated products are strongly preferred
  - **SA-10**:
    - for JAB authorizations, track security flaws and flaw resolution and report findings to organization-defined personnel, **to include FedRAMP**
  - **SA-11**:
    - static code analysis results documented
    - Continuous Monitoring Plan must describe how newly developed code is reviewed
  - **PE-3**:
    - inventories physical access devices **at least annually**
    - changes combinations and keys **at least annually**
  - **PE-6**:
    - reviews physical access logs **at least monthly**
  - **PE-8**:
    - visitor access records retained for a minimum of **one (1) year**
    - visitor access records reviewed **at least monthly**
  - **PE-14**:
    - temperature and humidity monitored **continuously**
    - service provider measures temperature at **server inlets** and humidity levels by **dew point**
  - **MP-6 (2)**:
    - sanitization equipment and procedures tested **at least annually**
  - **PS-3**:
    - national security clearance reinvestigation schedules:
      - **top secret**: fifth (5th) year
      - **secret**: tenth (10th) year
      - **confidential**: fifteenth (15th) year
    - **moderate risk law enforcement** and **high impact public trust level**: fifth (5th) year
    - no reinvestigation for other moderate risk positions or any low risk positions
  - **PS-4**:
    - disables information system access within **same day**
  - **PS-5**:
    - notifies organization-defined personnel or roles within **five days of the formal transfer action** (**DoD 24 hours**)
  - **PS-7**:
    - third-party personnel transfers/terminations notification within **same day**
  - **AT-1**:
    - policy review/update **at least every 3 years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **AT-2**:
    - security awareness training **at least annually**
  - **AT-3**:
    - role-based security training **at least annually**
  - **AT-4**:
    - training records retained **at least one year**
  - **AU-1**:
    - audit and accountability policy review/update **at every 3 years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **AU-2**:
    - auditable events include:
      - successful and unsuccessful account logon events
      - account management events
      - object access
      - policy change
      - privilege functions
      - process tracking
      - system events
      - for web applications: all administrator activity, authentication checks, authorization checks, data deletions, data access, data changes, permission changes
    - audited events are a subset of AU-2(a) and audited continually for each identified event
    - coordination between service provider and consumer documented and accepted by **JAB/AO**
  - **AU-2 (3)**:
    - reviewed/updated **annually or whenever there is a change in the threat environment**
    - guidance says annually or whenever threat environment changes are communicated by **JAB/AO**
  - **AU-3 (1)**:
    - audit record types defined to include:
      - session, connection, transaction, or activity duration
      - for client-server transactions, number of bytes received and bytes sent
      - additional informational messages to diagnose or identify the event
      - characteristics that describe or identify the object or resource being acted upon
    - audit record types approved and accepted by **JAB**
  - **AU-6**:
    - reviews/analyzes audit records **at least weekly**
    - coordination between service provider and consumer documented and accepted by the **Authorizing Official**
    - multi-tenant environments must document capability and means for review/analysis/reporting to consumer for consumer data
  - **AU-8 (1)**:
    - compares internal clocks with authoritative time source at **least hourly**
    - time source URL: **http://tf.nist.gov/tf-cgi/servers.cgi**
    - secondary time server selected from a different geographic region than primary
  - **AU-9 (2)**:
    - backs up audit records **at least weekly**
  - **AU-11**:
    - retains audit records for **at least ninety (90) days**
    - audit records kept on-line at least 90 days and further preserved off-line in accordance with **NARA requirements**
  - **AC-7**:
    - not more than **three (3)** consecutive invalid logon attempts during **fifteen (15) minutes**
    - when exceeded, locks account/node for **thirty (30) minutes** or delays next logon prompt according to organization-defined delay algorithm
  - **AC-8**:
    - system use notification elements require approval/acceptance by **JAB/AO**
    - verification and periodicity require approval/acceptance by **JAB/AO**
    - if not part of configuration baseline check, documented agreement on verification results and periodicity approved/accepted by **JAB/AO**
  - **AC-10**:
    - concurrent sessions limited to **three (3)** sessions for privileged access and **two (2)** sessions for non-privileged access
  - **AC-11**:
    - session lock after **fifteen (15) minutes** of inactivity or upon user request
  - **AC-17 (9)**:
    - remote access can be disconnected/disabled within **fifteen (15) minutes**
  - **AC-19 (5)**:
    - mobile device encryption options: **full-device encryption**; **container encryption**
  - **AC-22**:
    - review of public content for nonpublic information **at least quarterly**
  - **CM-1**:
    - configuration management policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **CM-2 (1)**:
    - baseline configuration review/update **at least annually**
    - when required due to **to include when directed by the JAB**
    - as an integral part of installations and upgrades
  - **CM-2 (3)**:
    - retains previous versions of baseline configurations to support rollback
  - **CM-2 (7)**:
    - issues configurations to individuals traveling to significant-risk locations; applies security safeguards when individuals return
  - **CM-3**:
    - retains records of configuration-controlled changes for organization-defined time period
    - coordinates and provides oversight through FedRAMP-required means
    - central means of communicating major changes/developments must be approved and accepted by **JAB/AO**
  - **CM-5 (5)**:
    - reviews and reevaluates privileges **at least quarterly**
  - **CM-6**:
    - configuration settings use **Center for Internet Security guidelines (Level 1)** or own settings if USGCB not available
    - checklist requirements: **SCAP validated** or **SCAP compatible**
  - **CM-7 (1)**:
    - review **at least Monthly**
  - **CM-7 (2)**:
    - program execution prevented through technical whitelist-like enforcement
  - **CM-7 (5)**:
    - reviews and updates authorized software list **at least annually or when there is a change**
  - **CM-8**:
    - inventory reviewed/updated **at least monthly**
    - inventory must be provided at least monthly or when there is a change
  - **CM-8 (3)**:
    - automated detection of unauthorized hardware/software/firmware with maximum **five-minute delay in detection**
  - **CP-3**:
    - contingency training within **ten (10) days** of assuming role/responsibility
    - thereafter **at least annually**
  - **CP-7**:
    - alternate processing site time period must be consistent with recovery time objectives and business impact analysis
  - **CP-8**:
    - alternate telecommunications time period consistent with recovery time objectives and business impact analysis
  - **CP-9**:
    - backups:
      - user-level information: **daily incremental; weekly full**
      - system-level information: **daily incremental; weekly full**
      - documentation including security-related documentation: **daily incremental; weekly full**
    - at least **three backup copies** of user-level information, system-level information, and documentation, with at least one online
  - **CP-9 (1)**:
    - backup information tested **at least annually**
  - **IA-1**:
    - identification and authentication policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **IA-2 (1)**:
    - multifactor authentication for network access to privileged accounts
  - **IA-2 (2)**:
    - multifactor authentication for network access to non-privileged accounts
  - **IA-2 (3)**:
    - multifactor authentication for local access to privileged accounts
  - **IA-2 (11)**:
    - remote access MFA for privileged and non-privileged accounts
    - one factor must be provided by a separate device
    - separate device must meet **FIPS 140-2, NIAP Certification, or NSA approval**
    - guidance says PIV = separate device; references **NIST SP 800-157**
  - **IA-2 (12)**:
    - accepts and electronically verifies **PIV credentials**
    - guidance says include **Common Access Card (CAC)**, the DoD technical implementation of PIV/FIPS 201/HSPD-12
  - **IA-4**:
    - prevent reuse of identifiers for **at least two (2) years**
    - disable user identifiers after **ninety days**
  - **IA-5**:
    - authenticators comply with **NIST SP 800-63-3 Digital Identity Guidelines IAL, AAL, FAL level 2**
  - **IA-5 (1)**:
    - password reuse prohibited for **twenty-four (24)** generations
    - changed characters requirement at least **one (1)**
  - **IA-5 (3)**:
    - registration for hardware/biometric multifactor authenticators conducted **in person**
  - **IA-8 (2)**:
    - accepts only **FICAM-approved third-party credentials**
  - **IR-1**:
    - incident response policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **IR-2**:
    - incident response training within organization-defined time period of assuming role
    - thereafter **at least annually**
  - **IR-3**:
    - incident response tests **at least annually**
    - test plans follow **NIST SP 800-61 (as amended)**
  - **IR-6**:
    - report suspected incidents within **US-CERT incident reporting timelines as specified in NIST SP800-61 (as amended)**
    - report according to **FedRAMP Incident Communications Procedure**
  - **MA-1**:
    - maintenance policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **MA-2**:
    - maintenance records include organization-defined maintenance-related information
    - personnel must explicitly approve removal from facilities for off-site maintenance/repairs
  - **MA-5 (1)**:
    - only MA-5(1)(a)(1) is required by FedRAMP
  - **MP-1**:
    - media protection policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **MP-3**:
    - exempted from marking: **no removable media types**
    - second parameter in MP‑3(b)-2 is **Not applicable**
  - **MP-4**:
    - controlled areas within facilities defined by the service provider
  - **MP-5**:
    - digital media transport protection uses **encryption using a FIPS 140-2 validated encryption module**
    - non-digital media transport protection uses **secured in locked container**
    - security measures approved and accepted by **JAB/AO**
  - **MP-6 (2)**:
    - sanitization tests **at least annually**
  - **PE-1**:
    - physical/environmental protection policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **PE-2**:
    - access list reviewed **at least annually**
  - **PE-3**:
    - entry/exit points, guards, access control systems/devices, and visitor monitoring requirements
    - physical access devices inventoried **at least annually**
    - combinations and keys changed **at least annually**
  - **PE-6 (1)**:
    - monitors physical intrusion alarms and surveillance equipment
  - **PE-8**:
    - visitor access records retained minimum **one (1) year**
    - reviewed **at least monthly**
  - **PE-14**:
    - temperature and humidity monitoring **continuously**
  - **PL-1**:
    - security planning policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **PL-2**:
    - security plan reviewed **at least annually**
    - security plan reviewed and approved by authorizing official or designated representative prior to implementation
  - **PL-4**:
    - rules of behavior review/update **at least every three (3) years**
  - **PL-8**:
    - information security architecture review/update **at least annually or when a significant change occurs**
    - significant change defined in **NIST SP 800-37 Revision 1, Appendix F, on Page F-8**
  - **PS-1**:
    - personnel security policy review/update **at least every three (3) years**
    - procedures review/update **at least annually**
  - **PS-2**:
    - position risk designations reviewed/revised **at least every three (3) years**
  - **PS-3**:
    - rescreening frequencies listed above
  - **PS-4**:
    - exit interview includes organization-defined information security topics
  - **PS-5**:
    - notification within **five days** of formal transfer action (**DoD 24 hours**)
  - **PS-6**:
    - access agreements reviewed/updated **at least annually**
  - **PS-7**:
    - third-party providers must notify organization-defined personnel or roles of transfers/terminations of third-party personnel who possess organizational credentials/badges or privileges within **same day**
  - **PS-8**:
    - notifications sent to organization-defined personnel or roles within organization-defined time period when sanctions process initiated

- “system security or privacy officer”: “An individual responsible for ensuring that the security and privacy posture is maintained for an organizational system and works in close collaboration with the system owner.”
- “systems security or privacy engineer”: “An individual, group, or organization responsible for conducting systems security or privacy engineering activities as part of the SDLC.” | | Exact “system security officer” / “system privacy officer” definitions | - “system security officer”: “Individual with assigned responsibility for maintaining the appropriate operational security posture for an information system or program.”
- “system privacy officer”: “Individual with assigned responsibility for maintaining the appropriate operational privacy posture for a system or program.” | | Exact field names / labels from task summaries | - “Potential Inputs”
- “Expected Outputs”

title: ISO 27001 RACI matrix | How to use it for implementation? - Advisera
content:
### RACI / responsibility matrix basics
- **RACI** is “a form of responsibility assignment presentation,” named after:
  - **Responsible**
  - **Accountable**
  - **Consulted**
  - **Informed**
- **Responsible:** “Refers to those who do the work to complete the task.”
- **Accountable:** “Designates the person who ultimately answer for the results of an activity, and also who delegates the work to the people who will execute it.”
- **Consulted:** “Refers to those who sought be heard on the related activity, and with whom there is two-way communication.”
- **Informed:** “Designates those who sought to be kept up-to-date on the progress of the activity, and with whom there is just one-way communication.”
- “In some situations, the same role that is accountable for an activity may also be responsible for its execution.”

### ISO 27001 RACI matrix roles
- **Top management**
- **Project Team**
- **Unit Heads / Process Owners / Interested Parties**
- **Employees / Users**

### ISO 27001 RACI matrix activities and assignments

| Activities | Top management | Project Team | Unit Heads / Process Owners / Interested Parties | Employees / Users |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Identifying the Information Security Management System (ISMS) requirements and interested parties | A | R | C | C |
| Defining ISMS basic framework (e.g., scope, policy, etc.) | A | R | C | I |
| Development of the risk assessment and treatment methodology | A | R | C | I |
| Performing the risk assessment and defining the risk treatment plan | A | R | C | C |
| Controls implementation | I | R | A | I |
| Training and awareness of personnel | I | R | A | I |
| Controls operation | I | R | A/R | R |
| Performance monitoring and measurement | I | R | A/R | R |
| Performing the internal audit | I | A/R | C | C |
| Performing management review | A | R | C | I |
| Addressing nonconformities, corrective actions, and opportunities for improvement | A | R | R | I |

### Legend
- **R** – Responsible
- **A** – Accountable
- **C** – Consulted
- **I** – Informed

### Documenting the RACI matrix
- The RACI matrix can be documented:
  - as a separate document, or
  - as part of the **Project Plan**
- Regarding the person responsible for obtaining top management buy-in for the project, “normally the plan’s author would be that person (sometimes known as the project sponsor).”
- Specific details about these responsibilities should be documented in project documents “if such exist,” including:
  - schedule
  - budget
  - communication plan
  - other documents developed as part of the ISO 27001 implementation
- When a role is designated as **“A/R”**:
  - besides accountability, that role will also have “a management action to perform regarding that activity”
- A single **“R”** means:
  - “the performance of an operational aspect of the activity”

### Explicit example given for A/R and R
- For **performance monitoring and measurement**:
  - “the head of the department is responsible for reviewing the measurement results and defining the proper actions”
  - “employees have the responsibility to perform the measurements and carry out the actions decided by the head of the department”

### Top management buy-in / approval / escalation conventions
- The information security roles and responsibilities matrix was developed assuming that the project already has **top management buy-in**
- “Obtaining the management buy-in is critical to the success of the project”
- In terms of the RACI matrix, obtaining management buy-in:
  - “would only add unnecessary complexity”
- “Obtaining management approval is only done once before the project planning and execution start”
- This activity can be defined “within other planning documents of the project”
- The article states top management involvement happens “mostly at the beginning and at the end of the project”

### Role-specific note from the article
- By defining **Unit Heads / Process Owners / Interested Parties** as **Accountable** for phases related to:
  - controls implementation
  - measurement
- the organization can “enforce and maintain their commitment to the project”

### Absent from the page
- No security operations roles beyond the listed ISO 27001 project roles
- No task ownership fields, ticket fields, SLAs, playbooks, or reviewer/authorization workflow fields
- No escalation matrix beyond the stated top management approval/buy-in timing and A/R explanation
description: A RACI matrix helps you define clear roles and responsibilities - a critical success factor of an ISO 27001 implementation project. Learn more about it.

title: ISO 27001 Clause 5.3: Roles & Responsibilities | TCSA
content:
| Category | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Clause requirement | Top management must ensure that the responsibilities and authorities for every role relevant to information security are assigned and communicated within the organization. |
| Clause requirement | The people holding each role need to know what they own and what authority they carry to act on it, and everyone else needs to know who to go to. |
| Specific required assignment | Top management must give someone the responsibility and authority for ensuring the ISMS conforms to the requirements of ISO 27001 itself. |
| Specific required assignment | Top management must give someone the responsibility and authority for reporting on the performance of the ISMS back to top management. |
| Specific required assignment | The two duties may sit with one person or be split across several. |
| Specific required assignment | Top management may additionally assign responsibility for reporting ISMS performance more widely within the organization. |
| Prohibition | Leaving either duty unassigned or implied is not permitted. |
| Purpose | The clause exists to guarantee the ISMS has named, empowered owners so that conformance to the standard and honest performance reporting to top management never depend on assumption or goodwill. |
| Common role structure mentioned | ISMS manager or CISO who runs the system day to day. |
| Common role structure mentioned | Risk owners who accept or treat individual risks. |
| Common role structure mentioned | Asset owners accountable for specific information and systems. |
| Common role structure mentioned | Control owners who keep individual safeguards operating. |
| Common role structure mentioned | An internal auditor who must stay independent of what they audit. |
| Common role structure mentioned | Top management itself retains accountability it can never delegate. |
| Standard scope statement | None of these titles are mandated; the standard cares about the duties being owned, not what the owner is called. |
| Auditor focus | Auditors check the two explicitly required assignments by name: who ensures the ISMS conforms to the standard, and who reports its performance to top management. |
| Typical assignment | The first duty usually lands on the ISMS manager or CISO. |
| Typical assignment | The second is evidenced most convincingly through management review. |
| Evidence of performance reporting | The named person presenting metrics, audit results, and incidents to leadership, with minutes to prove it. |
| RACI use | For everything else, a RACI matrix is the workhorse artifact. |
| RACI definition | Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. |
| RACI structure | One axis lists ISMS duties, the other lists roles, and the intersections leave accountability nowhere to hide. |
| Auditor test | Auditors ask the named people what they own and compare the answer to the matrix. |
| Auditor test | Auditors ask employees nowhere near the security team who they would report an incident to. |
| Conformity risk | Assignment that was never communicated, or communication that did not survive the last reorganization, is where conformity actually breaks. |
| Failure examples | Orphaned controls: safeguards keep running only as long as the volunteer who set them up stays; the first resignation breaks them silently. |
| Failure examples | Invisible ISMS decay: with no one assigned to report performance, top management learns about problems from audit findings or incidents instead of from its own system. |
| Failure examples | Stalled incident response: teams lose critical hours establishing who has the authority to isolate systems, engage counsel, or notify a regulator. |
| Failure examples | Leadership-level nonconformities: missing or unevidenced assignments surface at Stage 1, and a named owner who cannot describe their own duties converts the gap into a major finding at Stage 2. |
| Failure examples | Single-person dependency: when who-does-what lives in one head instead of documented assignments, every departure causes a small organizational amnesia. |

### Documented information required
| Item | Status | Extracted facts |
|---|---|---|
| ISMS roles, responsibilities and authorities matrix (RACI) | Recommended | Clause 5.3 names no mandatory document, but a RACI or roles matrix is how virtually every certified organization evidences assignment. |
| ISMS roles, responsibilities and authorities matrix (RACI) | Recommended | ISMS duties on one axis, roles on the other, with named persons, effective dates, and the two clause-mandated responsibilities explicitly placed. |
| Appointment records and job descriptions with security responsibilities | Recommended | Appointment letters, management minutes naming the ISMS owner, and role profiles that embed security duties prove the assignments were made formally and survive personnel changes far better than tribal knowledge. |
| Organization chart with ISMS reporting lines | Recommended | A current chart showing how the security function reports toward top management. |
| Organization chart with ISMS reporting lines | Recommended | Auditors use it to verify the performance-reporting line the clause requires actually exists and is not buried under conflicting interests. |

### Implementation steps
| Step | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| 1 | Inventory the duties before naming the people. |
| 1 | List every recurring activity the ISMS needs: risk assessments, policy maintenance, access reviews, incident coordination, supplier reviews, awareness training, internal audit, metrics and reporting. |
| 1 | Build the list from your processes and your Statement of Applicability. |
| 1 | Define it as roles, not individuals, so the structure survives turnover. |
| 2 | Make the two mandated assignments explicit. |
| 2 | Top management must formally assign who ensures the ISMS conforms to ISO 27001 and who reports ISMS performance back to them. |
| 2 | Record the assignment in an appointment letter or management meeting minutes with a date and signature. |
| 2 | One person may hold both duties, but neither may be left implied. |
| 3 | Appoint risk owners and asset owners by name. |
| 3 | Every risk in the register and every significant asset needs an owner with real authority to make decisions about it. |
| 3 | Decision areas explicitly listed: budget, process change, acceptance. |
| 3 | “The IT department” is not an owner; a named role held by a named person is. |
| 4 | Build the RACI matrix and resolve the conflicts it exposes. |
| 4 | Map duties to roles as Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. |
| 4 | The exercise will surface conflicts such as the same person operating a control and auditing it, or approving their own exceptions. |
| 4 | These conflicts feed directly into segregation-of-duties analysis under control A.5.3. |
| 4 | Resolve each conflict, or document the compensating measure. |
| 5 | Protect independence where headcount is thin. |
| 5 | Internal audit must never review the auditor's own work. |
| 5 | In small organizations this means cross-training someone outside the security function, swapping audit duties between departments, or outsourcing internal audit entirely. |
| 5 | Whatever the model, record why it preserves objectivity. |
| 6 | Communicate the assignments, provably. |
| 6 | Publish the roles matrix on the intranet. |
| 6 | Embed duties in job descriptions. |
| 6 | Cover who-owns-what in onboarding and awareness sessions. |
| 6 | Announce changes when they happen. |
| 6 | Keep the artifacts: the published page, the session deck, the acknowledgment records. |
| 7 | Review assignments on change and at planned intervals. |
| 7 | Tie the matrix to your joiner-mover-leaver process so departures and role changes trigger an update. |
| 7 | Review it at least annually. |
| 7 | A standing management review agenda item works well. |
| 7 | A matrix that still names employees who left two reorganizations ago is the most common Clause 5.3 finding. |

### Audit evidence
| Evidence type | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Documentation | Roles and responsibilities matrix (RACI) covering ISMS duties, with named persons and effective dates. |
| Documentation | Appointment letter or management minutes assigning ISMS conformance ownership and performance reporting to top management. |
| Documentation | Job descriptions or role profiles that embed information security responsibilities. |
| Documentation | Organization chart showing the security function's reporting line toward top management. |
| Documentation | Management review minutes showing the assigned person actually reporting ISMS performance. |
| Interviews | Top management on how they assigned the two mandated responsibilities and what authority they delegated with them. |
| Interviews | The ISMS manager or CISO on the duties they own, the authority they carry, and how they report performance upward. |
| Interviews | Employees outside the security team on who they would report an incident to and where role information is published. |
| Observations | The intranet page, handbook, or portal where ISMS roles are published and visible to staff. |
| Observations | A live comparison of the roles matrix against the current organization chart, looking for post-reorganization drift. |
| Observations | The performance-reporting trail in action — management review decks, dashboards, or recordings showing the named owner presenting. |

### Regional compliance context
| Region | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| India | Significant Data Fiduciaries under the DPDP Act 2023 must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India. |
| India | CERT-In's directions require organizations to designate a point of contact for incident reporting. |
| India | RBI expects regulated entities to designate a senior CISO whose role stays independent of day-to-day IT operations. |
| India | Map these statutory roles into your Clause 5.3 matrix rather than running them as a parallel structure. |
| Gulf | Saudi Arabia's PDPL requires controllers to designate a personal data protection officer in defined cases. |
| Gulf | SAMA-regulated financial institutions must maintain a dedicated cybersecurity function with a named head. |
| Gulf | A single roles matrix showing both the ISO 27001 assignments and the statutory appointments is the cleanest way to evidence all of them at once. |

### Practitioner insights
| Source | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Practitioner insight | The organization may have a beautifully formatted roles matrix, but the person named as ISMS owner cannot state the two responsibilities Clause 5.3 actually required top management to assign: conformance and performance reporting. |
| Practitioner insight | Cross-check 5.3 against the Clause 9.3 management review minutes. |
| Practitioner insight | If the named person never appears as the presenter or author of the performance inputs, the assignment exists only on paper. |
| Practitioner insight | Make sure the people named can describe their duties in their own words, and that the reporting duty leaves a visible trail to top management. |
| Practitioner insight | In small companies, one person wearing four ISMS hats is normal and acceptable; the standard never says otherwise. |
| Practitioner insight | The same person operating a control, auditing that control, and approving their own exceptions is where combined roles cross into a segregation problem. |
| Practitioner insight | Write down which roles are combined, state the conflict honestly, and name the compensating measure. |
| Practitioner insight | Example compensating measures listed: an outsourced internal audit, a counter-signature from the founder, a peer review. |
| Practitioner insight | Auditors respect a documented conflict with a mitigation more than an org chart pretending a ten-person startup has six independent functions. |

### Common challenges and solutions
| Challenge | Solution |
|---|---|
| Roles are defined in a policy document nobody reads, and staff cannot name a single ISMS owner when asked. | Move the assignments out of the policy annex and into the places people actually look: the security intranet page, onboarding decks, and team channels. Announce changes when they happen, and spot-test awareness quarterly with a two-question pulse check — who owns the ISMS, and where do incidents go. If staff fail the spot test, the problem is your channel, not their memory. |
| In a 20-person startup the founder or CTO holds every security role, and the auditor questions whether any of it is independent. | Combining roles is acceptable; combining conflicting ones is not. Keep internal audit independent by outsourcing it or training someone outside the security function, separate exception approval from exception requesting, and document the remaining conflicts with their compensating measures. A short conflict analysis signed by management turns an awkward Stage 2 conversation into a closed question. |
| The roles matrix drifts — it still names employees who resigned, and the reorganization six months ago appears nowhere in it. | Make the matrix an output of your joiner-mover-leaver process rather than a standalone artifact: every leaver and role-change ticket includes an “update ISMS roles” step. Add an annual full review as a management review agenda item, and keep the matrix under version control so the trail of changes is self-evident at audit. |
| The ISMS manager is accountable for conformance but has no authority. | Authority is half of what Clause 5.3 requires top management to assign, so fix it at the source. Issue an appointment letter that states the mandate explicitly, define an escalation path that terminates at top management, and give the role a standing slot in leadership meetings. |
| ISMS performance reaches leadership informally — hallway conversations and ad hoc emails that leave no audit evidence. | Give the reporting duty a fixed form and rhythm: a quarterly ISMS report or dashboard covering risks, incidents, audit findings, and objective progress, presented by the named owner and minuted. The Clause 9.3 management review is the natural anchor, but do not let it be the only touchpoint. |

### Frequently asked questions
| Question | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| What is the difference between Clause 5.3 and Annex A control A.5.2? | Clause 5.3 is a mandatory management-system requirement: top management must assign and communicate ISMS roles, including conformance ownership and performance reporting. A.5.2 is the Annex A control that extends the same discipline to every security duty in the organization, applied according to your Statement of Applicability. In practice one well-built roles matrix usually evidences both. |
| Does ISO 27001 require us to appoint a CISO? | No. The standard requires responsibilities and authorities to be assigned but never mandates job titles. An ISMS manager, an information security officer, or a director wearing the hat part-time all satisfy the clause if the duties and authority are real. Sector regulators can be stricter: RBI-regulated entities in India and SAMA-regulated entities in Saudi Arabia are expected to designate a CISO regardless of what ISO 27001 says. |
| Can one person hold multiple ISMS roles in a small company? | Yes — combining roles is normal below roughly 50 employees, and auditors expect it. The limits are conflicts: nobody should audit their own work, approve their own access or exceptions, or be the sole reviewer of controls they operate. Document which roles are combined, why, and what compensating measure covers each conflict, and the combination becomes defensible. |
| Is a RACI matrix mandatory for Clause 5.3? | No — Clause 5.3 carries no named documented-information requirement, so no specific document is mandated. You must still evidence that assignments were made and communicated, and a RACI matrix is the cleanest single artifact for both. Role descriptions in job profiles, appointment letters, and a published responsibilities page also work, as long as together they cover assignment, authority, and communication. |
| Who should the ISMS manager report to? | As directly to top management as your structure allows. The clause requires someone to report ISMS performance to top management, which is hard to evidence if the security function sits three layers down inside IT operations. A reporting line to the CEO, board, or risk committee, exercised through management review, is the pattern auditors read as healthy. |
| How do auditors actually test Clause 5.3? | At Stage 1 they check the documents: assignments exist, the two mandated responsibilities are placed, and the structure matches your scope. At Stage 2 they test reality by interviewing the named owners about their duties and authority, asking random staff who they would report an incident to, and cross-checking management review minutes to confirm the performance-reporting duty is exercised. The fastest route to a finding is a named owner who cannot describe their own role. |
description: Assigning and communicating ISMS roles — who operates it, who reports on its performance, and how authority is delegated.
author: Tranquility Cybersecurity; Surendra Pal Singh; Saundhi Chauhan; Parth Chauhan

title: ISO 27001 A.5.2: Security Roles & Responsibilities | TCSA
content:
| Category | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Control Definition | The organization must work out which information security roles and responsibilities it needs, define them, and allocate each to specific people or teams — scaled to fit its own size, structure, and requirements. |
| Control Objective | To ensure clear accountability for information security by defining and documenting security roles, assigning responsibilities to specific individuals or teams, and establishing reporting structures so everyone knows who is responsible for what aspects of information security. |
| RACI definitions | Responsible (does the work); Accountable (ultimate ownership, one person only); Consulted (provides input); Informed (kept updated). |
| Required documentation methods | Job descriptions or RACI matrices (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed); security charter; responsibility matrix. |
| Required assignment principle | Assign security responsibilities to specific positions, not just generic "IT team". |
| Reporting structure requirement | Establish reporting lines showing who security roles report to. |
| Review requirement | Periodically review role definitions ensuring they match current organizational structure and security needs. |
| Purpose of role clarity | Clear accountability ensuring no security responsibility is orphaned. |

- Information security roles and responsibilities means clearly defining who does what for security in the organization: who approves security policies, who monitors security alerts, who responds to incidents, who manages user access, who conducts security awareness training, and who is ultimately accountable.
- Specific examples of security roles mentioned:
  - CISO provides strategic direction
  - security analysts monitor threats
  - IT implements controls
  - data owners classify information
  - all employees follow security policies

| Implementation guidance step | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| 1. Identify Required Information Security Roles | Define needed security roles based on organization size and complexity: CISO or Information Security Manager (strategic direction, policy ownership, board reporting); Security Analyst/Engineer (technical implementation, monitoring, incident response); IT Security Administrator (access management, security tool administration); Data Protection Officer (DPDPA compliance, privacy governance); Security Awareness Coordinator (training programs); Incident Response Lead; Business Continuity Manager; Third-Party Risk Manager. Small organizations may combine roles; large organizations may have specialized teams. |
| 2. Document Responsibilities for Each Security Role | Create detailed responsibility definitions using RACI matrix. For each security control and activity, specify who implements, who approves, who reviews, who escalates issues. Example for user access management: IT Admin is Responsible for provisioning accounts; Data Owner is Accountable for approving access; Security team is Consulted for privilege escalation; Audit team is Informed of changes. Document in role descriptions, security charter, or responsibility matrix. |
| 3. Assign Security Roles to Specific Individuals | Map defined roles to actual people, not generic titles. Assign CISO role to specific executive (name, email, phone); designate security analysts by name; identify data owners for each information system or data category; appoint security champions in each business unit. For critical roles, designate backups for continuity during absences. Update organizational charts showing security reporting lines. Communicate assignments formally via email and include in individual job descriptions during performance reviews. |
| 4. Establish Security Reporting Structure and Governance | Define reporting hierarchy: CISO reports to CEO or Board, not buried under CTO/CIO; security team reports to CISO; security champions report to CISO with dotted line to business units. Establish governance bodies: Security Steering Committee (executive-level, quarterly, approves policies and budgets), Security Operations Committee (tactical-level, monthly, reviews incidents and metrics), and working groups for specific initiatives. Document decision-making authority: who can approve policy exceptions, who authorizes security spending, who declares security incidents. |
| 5. Include Security Responsibilities in Job Descriptions | Update job descriptions to include specific security duties. Examples: Security Analyst: monitor SIEM alerts, conduct vulnerability scans; IT Administrator: provision accounts per security policy, review access quarterly; All Employees: complete security awareness training, report suspicious emails, protect credentials. Include security responsibilities in performance objectives and annual reviews. |
| 6. Clarify Business Unit and Data Owner Responsibilities | Define business roles including Data Owners (department heads responsible for classifying data, approving access, defining retention), System Owners (application owners accountable for security of their systems), Process Owners (responsible for security of business processes), and Information Asset Owners (accountable for protection of specific information types). |
| 7. Review and Update Roles Periodically | Conduct annual role review: verify assigned individuals still hold positions, update for organizational changes (mergers, restructuring, new systems requiring data owners), assess if role definitions match current security needs (cloud adoption may require new cloud security role), and confirm role holders understand their responsibilities. When employees change positions, immediately transfer security responsibilities and revoke previous access. Document role changes in security management reviews. |

| Audit evidence type | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Documentation | Organization chart showing security roles and reporting lines; RACI matrix or responsibility assignment matrix for information security; Job descriptions including security responsibilities for key roles; Security charter or governance document defining roles and decision authority; Security Steering Committee charter with member roles and responsibilities. |
| Interviews | CISO about security role definitions and how responsibilities are communicated; Role holders about their understanding of security responsibilities; HR about how security is incorporated into job descriptions and performance reviews. |
| Observations | Review organizational charts confirming security reporting structure; Verification that security activities have specific assigned owners; Demonstration of how security responsibilities are tracked and monitored; Evidence of role reviews and updates when organizational changes occur. |

- Without defined security roles and responsibilities, organizations face:
  - Security Tasks Neglected – Critical activities like reviewing access logs, applying security patches, or conducting security awareness training are skipped because no specific person is accountable
  - Delayed Incident Response – When breach occurs, confusion about who should respond, who has authority to make decisions, and who communicates with stakeholders wastes precious hours
  - Compliance Audit Failures – ISO 27001, SOC 2 auditors require documented security roles; inability to show who is responsible for controls results in non-conformities
  - Conflicting Decisions – Multiple people making security decisions without clear authority leads to inconsistent policies, circumvented controls, and security chaos
  - Ineffective Security Committees – Security steering committees without defined decision rights become discussion forums that produce no actual security improvements

- Indian organizations often lack dedicated security teams, leading to security being "everyone's responsibility" (which means no one's responsibility).
- Security roles do not require full-time positions: assign Information Security Manager responsibility to existing IT Manager or senior engineer (10-20% of time), outsource technical security to managed security service provider (MSSP), use virtual CISO (vCISO) consultants for strategic guidance quarterly, and leverage security champions model (train one person per department as security point of contact).
- Better to have explicitly assigned part-time owner than implicitly assumed full-time non-owner.

| Challenge | Solution |
|---|---|
| Small organizations cannot afford dedicated security team or CISO. | Assign Information Security Manager responsibility to existing IT Manager or senior engineer (10-20% of time), outsource technical security to MSSP, use vCISO consultants for strategic guidance quarterly, and leverage security champions model. Document role assignments clearly even if part-time. |
| Business units resist taking on data owner responsibilities claiming they lack security expertise. | Data ownership is business decision, not technical: data owner classifies data sensitivity based on business impact, approves who should have access based on job needs, and defines retention based on business/legal requirements. Security team provides guidance, templates, and training but business retains accountability. Make this expectation explicit in executive job descriptions. Escalate to CEO if departments refuse ownership. |
| Multiple people claim to be responsible for same security task creating confusion and duplication. | Apply RACI discipline strictly: for every security activity, exactly one person/role is Accountable. Use RACI matrix workshops to resolve conflicts: gather stakeholders, list security activities down rows and roles across columns, assign R/A/C/I for each intersection, resolve disagreements before publishing. Update matrix when conflicts arise. |
| When security roles change hands, successor does not understand or inherit responsibilities properly. | Create role transition procedure: document critical security responsibilities, access requirements, recurring tasks with schedules (monthly access reviews, quarterly policy updates), key contacts and escalation paths, and ongoing projects/initiatives. Require knowledge transfer session, update access permissions immediately, and notify stakeholders of role change. |
| Security responsibilities defined but not enforced; people ignore assigned duties with no consequences. | Integrate into performance management: include security responsibilities in annual objectives and OKRs, measure security task completion (access reviews conducted on time, training completion rates, incident response participation), link to performance ratings and bonuses, and have managers hold directs accountable. Use metrics and visible dashboards. |

- Big mistake noted: CISO reporting to CTO or CIO instead of CEO/Board creates conflict of interest.
- ISO 27001 clause 5.3 requires that ISMS performance is reported to top management.
- An independent reporting line for the security lead is described as the cleanest way to show auditors that security concerns reach board level.

| FAQ topic | Extracted facts |
|---|---|
| Dedicated CISO requirement | ISO 27001 does not mandate title "CISO" but requires someone accountable for information security management system. Small organizations can assign Information Security Manager responsibility to existing role (CTO, IT Manager) if explicitly documented, sufficient time is allocated, and reporting line ensures independence. Combining with CTO is acceptable only if no conflict of interest exists and time is formally allocated. |
| CISO vs DPO | CISO focuses on information security (protecting confidentiality, integrity, availability of all information including non-personal data). DPO focuses on privacy (ensuring lawful processing of personal data per DPDPA, handling data principal requests and grievances, advising on DPIAs). DPDPA mandates DPO for significant data fiduciaries. Same person may fill both roles in smaller companies or separate roles in larger companies. |
| Data owner designation | Data owner should be senior business role who understands data business value and can make risk decisions: for customer data, head of sales or marketing; for financial data, CFO or finance controller; for HR data, CHRO; for product data, head of product. Data owner is accountable for classifying data, approving access, defining retention/disposal. IT implements data owner decisions but should not be data owner. |
| Cloud services and third-party SaaS | Shared responsibility model applies: define who is responsible for security aspects you control vs vendor controls. For IaaS (AWS, Azure): vendor secures physical infrastructure/hypervisor, you secure OS/applications/data—assign your staff as responsible. For SaaS (Salesforce): vendor secures application infrastructure, you secure user access/data classification—assign your admin as responsible. Create responsibility matrix for each cloud service mapping security tasks to roles. Include vendor in RACI as Responsible or Consulted for tasks they handle. |
| Confidentiality of role definitions | Security role definitions should be transparent, not confidential: publish security organizational chart, RACI matrix, and security charter so everyone knows who to contact for security questions/incidents. Individual compensation details remain confidential. Exception: highly sensitive roles (penetration testers, insider threat investigators) may limit publishing specific names for operational security. |
| Universal security responsibilities for all employees | (1) complete mandatory security awareness training annually, (2) protect authentication credentials and never share passwords, (3) report security incidents and suspicious activity immediately, (4) follow acceptable use policy for systems and data, (5) maintain physical security (lock screens when leaving desk, challenge unknown visitors, protect assets), (6) handle data according to classification labels. Document these baseline responsibilities in acceptable use policy signed by all employees during onboarding. |

- User access management example fields/responsibilities explicitly stated:
  - IT Admin: Responsible for provisioning accounts
  - Data Owner: Accountable for approving access
  - Security team: Consulted for privilege escalation
  - Audit team: Informed of changes

- Job-description examples explicitly stated:

  - IT Administrator: provision accounts per security policy, review access quarterly
  - All Employees: complete security awareness training, report suspicious emails, protect credentials

- Reporting structure explicitly stated:

  - security champions report to CISO with dotted line to business units

- Business roles explicitly stated:
  - Data Owners: department heads responsible for classifying data, approving access, defining retention
  - System Owners: application owners accountable for security of their systems
  - Process Owners: responsible for security of business processes
  - Information Asset Owners: accountable for protection of specific information types

- Role review explicitly stated:

  - verify assigned individuals still hold positions
  - update for mergers, restructuring, new systems requiring data owners
  - assess if cloud adoption may require new cloud security role
  - immediately transfer responsibilities and revoke previous access when employees change positions
  - document role changes in security management reviews

- Specific role assignment examples explicitly stated:
  - assign CISO role to specific executive with name, email, phone
  - designate security analysts by name
  - identify data owners for each information system or data category
  - appoint security champions in each business unit
  - designate backups for critical roles for continuity during absences

  - **Playbooks section**

  - **/ Suggest playbooks** skill

- **Playbooks / playbook behavior**
  - Playbooks are **step-by-step, actionable guides** that combine clear instructions with automation.
  - They help teams resolve work items consistently and efficiently by embedding standard operating procedures (**SOPs**) directly on the work item.
  - Available on Jira Service Management **Premium** and **Enterprise** plans.
  - They appear in a dedicated section on the work item.
  - For a playbook to show up:
    1. **Enable the feature** in **Project settings > Features**.
    2. **Create a playbook**.
    3. **Match visibility**: the playbook’s visibility (**work type**, **request type**, or **custom JQL**) must match the work item details.
  - **Tip:** Use **Playbook templates for Jira Service Management** to get started quickly for common **IT Operations**, **ITSM**, and **HRSM** scenarios.
  - When a work item matches a playbook’s criteria, the playbook appears in the **Playbooks** section.
  - Responders can:
    - **Follow instructional steps**
      - mark the step as **done**
      - mark the step as **undone**, if required
    - **Run automation flows**
      - provide inputs if prompted
    - **Review outputs**
      - see messages and results from automation
    - **Track execution log**
      - view who completed each step and the outputs
  - Playbooks help create standard operating procedures (**SOPs**) with automated steps.
  - Playbook metadata:
    - **Created by:** The project admin who authored the playbook.
    - **Last updated:** When the playbook was last republished.
    - **Usage details:** How often the playbook was used on work items in the last 30 days.

- **SLAs**
  - **Not explicitly stated on the page:** no SLA fields, SLA targets, or SLA escalation conventions are provided.

- **Reviewer / authorization responsibilities**
  - **Review suggestions and summaries** alongside your team’s expertise and organizational policies before acting.
  - **Review results with operational context.**
  - If suggestions seem off, **try refining your prompt or reviewing work item details for clarity**.
  - **Rovo suggests relevant playbooks** by analyzing:
    - **summary**
    - **description**
    - playbook usage signals
  - How Rovo ranks suggestions:
    - **Work item context:** keywords in the summary and description.
    - **Execution history:** how often a playbook was used on similar work items.
    - **Playbook metadata:** information in the playbook title and steps.
  - AI-suggested playbooks:
    - **do not run steps automatically**
    - **do not enforce actions**
    - **do not guarantee deterministic predictions**
  - **AI Playbook summarization uses only the playbook’s step details** to generate the summary.
  - It **does not analyze specific configurations or automation flows**.
  - **Your organization’s playbook data is never used** to generate suggestions or summaries for other Atlassian customers.

- **Exact AI / compliance statements**
  - **The AI-generated summary is not HIPAA compliant and must not be used to process PHI or other HIPAA-regulated data.**
  - **The Playbook Suggestion feature is not HIPAA compliant and must not be used to process PHI or other HIPAA-regulated data.**
  - **This AI feature is in beta.**
  - **AI-suggested Playbooks and AI-generated Summaries support decision-making but don’t replace human judgment.**
